questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presents with chest tightness, coughing, and wheezing for the past 2 days. His asthma has been well controlled with low-dose fluticasone inhaled twice a day and an albuterol metered-dose inhaler as needed, which he requires only about twice a month. He recently strained his calf during a basketball game and began using ibuprofen to alleviate the pain. His history is significant for sinus surgery 3 years ago to remove nasal polyps. A physical examination is significant for a healthy appearance and normal vital signs. Nasal polyps are appreciated bilaterally. Chest auscultation reveals diffuse wheezing. A musculoskeletal examination is normal. Which of the following strategies is most appropriate to recommend?
questions.stemHtml:
A 37-year-old man presents with chest tightness, coughing, and wheezing for the past 2 days. His asthma has been well controlled with low-dose fluticasone inhaled twice a day and an albuterol metered-dose inhaler as needed, which he requires only about twice a month. He recently strained his calf during a basketball game and began using ibuprofen to alleviate the pain. His history is significant for sinus surgery 3 years ago to remove nasal polyps. A physical examination is significant for a healthy appearance and normal vital signs. Nasal polyps are appreciated bilaterally. Chest auscultation reveals diffuse wheezing. A musculoskeletal examination is normal.
Which of the following strategies is most appropriate to recommend?

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain a limited CT scan of the sinuses

options.label: D
options.text: Conduct allergy testing for seasonal allergens

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Discontinue nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of aspirin-exacerbated (ASA) respiratory disease (AERD). His history of recurrent nasal polyps requiring surgery, asthma, and loss of asthma control after exposure to ASA or other NSAIDs is known as the Samter triad. Ingestion of any NSAID that inhibits COX-1 temporarily increases the formation or release of mediators, resulting in an exacerbation of disease in the respiratory tract. The clinical setting in which the physician should be most suspicious of AERD is in an asthmatic patient with the formation (often relentless) of nasal polyps and pansinusitis as confirmed by imaging procedures. Ingestion of ASA or NSAIDs can induce combinations of intense rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, injection of the conjunctivae, laryngospasm, and bronchospasm. Avoidance of ASA/NSAIDs is the foundation of therapy. Otherwise, asthma should be managed according to current guidelines, which were recently updated in the National Asthma Education Program Expert Panel Report 3. Incorrect Options: Option A - Start moderate-dose inhaled fluticasone: Starting moderate-dose inhaled fluticasone would be a reasonable option to consider for the management of asthma exacerbation, but it does not address the primary issue of ASA-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) caused by NSAID use. In this case, the patient's asthma exacerbation is likely triggered by the use of ibuprofen, so the most appropriate step is to discontinue the NSAID. Option B - Obtain a limited CT scan of the sinuses: Obtaining a limited CT scan of the sinuses may be useful for evaluating the extent of sinus disease in patients with AERD and chronic rhinosinusitis. However, it is not the first-line strategy to address the acute asthma exacerbation caused by NSAID use. The priority is to discontinue the NSAID. Option D - Conduct allergy testing for seasonal allergens: seasonal allergens may be helpful in managing asthma in patients with allergic triggers, but it does not address the acute asthma exacerbation triggered by NSAID use. The primary approach is to discontinue the NSAID and manage asthma according to guidelines @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hypoaldosteronism: Hypoaldosteronism is a condition in which there is a deficiency of aldosterone. Normally the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leads to the activation of aldosterone. The collecting duct of the nephron is the main site where the aldosterone acts. Normally aldosterone causes the excretion of hydrogen and potassium ions. However, in renal tubular acidosis type 4, there is a deficiency of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance, which results in hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia can be fatal to the heart and can result in life-threatening arrhythmias. With hyperkalemia, ECG changes can occur. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperaldosteronism: Hyperaldosteronism is the excessive aldosterone production that results in excessive excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. As a result, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is seen in such patients. Option C - ADH deficiency: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on vasopressin receptors that cause the expression of receptors in the distal part of nephrons causing the reabsorption of water. In ADH deficiency, there is insufficient ADH which results in excessive excretion of water leading to decreased urine osmolality and high serum osmolarity. Option D - SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is a condition in which there is excessive retention of water due to excess ADH. The urine osmolality is high and there is hypervolemia. Some of the causes of SIADH are meningitis, encephalitis, brain tumors, psychosis, lung disease, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A
options.text: Biallelic pathogenic variants of the SLC12A3 gene

questions.answerText: Biallelic pathogenic variants of the SLC12A3 gene
questions.solution: Correct Option A- B iallelic pathogenic variants of the SLC12A3 gene: The mutation causing Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive Defect in the SLC12A3 gene on chromosome 16p, causing the impaired function of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule and impaired Na+ and Cl- reabsorption causing mild natriuresis, mild volume depletion and mild RAAS activation. Incorrect Options: Option B- Mutations in SLC12A1: SLC12A1 gene mutation causes Barter Syndrome type 1. It encodes the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2). The defective NKCC2 function mimics the effects of loop diuretics, which blocks this pathway directly. Option C- Mutations in KCNJ1: Mutations in the KCNJ1 gene are responsible for causing Barter syndrome type 2 BS2. Option D- Mutations of the SLC4A1 gene: The Mutations of the SLC4A1 gene cause dominant distal Renal tubular acidosis . @Neet_pg_bot

She often complains of pain in the right lumbar area. The pain radiates from the loin to the groin. X-ray shows renal stones. Her PTH level is elevated. Which of the following set of biochemical findings correlates with the disease pathology
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of lethargy, malaise, dehydration, and depression that has been worsening for 1 week. She often complains of pain in the right lumbar area. The pain radiates from the loin to the groin. X-ray shows renal stones. Her PTH level is elevated. Which of the following set of biochemical findings correlates with the disease pathology
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia: Hypophosphatemia and hypercalcemia are the main biochemical findings observed in hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid hormone is the primary hormone that regulates calcium levels in the body. Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level . Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways: Bones It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone. At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption. Kidney Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity . Activates vitamin D. Intestine Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate. Factors affecting PTH level: Low magnesium elevates PTH Very low magnesium decreases PTH Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion. Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. Lab findings show: Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline. Calcium levels al s o decreased by about 25% from the baseline The level of uric acid may also be increased. Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin. Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia:

  • Hypophosphatemia and hypercalcemia are the main biochemical findings observed in hyperparathyroidism.
  • The parathyroid hormone is the primary hormone that regulates calcium levels in the body.
  • Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level.
  • Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways:
    • Bones
      • It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone.
      • At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption.
    • Kidney
      • Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity.
      • Activates vitamin D.
    • Intestine
      • Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate.
  • Factors affecting PTH level:
    • Low magnesium elevates PTH
    • Very low magnesium decreases PTH
    • Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion.
    • Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia:

  • Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream.
  • Lab findings show:
    • Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline.
    • Calcium levels also decreased by about 25% from the baseline
    • The level of uric acid may also be increased.

Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: 

  • High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin.

Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: 

  • Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids.

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Acute exacerbation: Acute exacerbation of asthma is a sudden and severe worsening of asthma symptoms, which can be life-threatening. It can be triggered by various factors such as exposure to allergens, infections, exercise, emotional stress, and medication non-adherence. The symptoms of acute exacerbation of asthma may include wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing, chest tightness, and difficulty in breathing. During an acute exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, swollen, and narrowed, making it difficult for air to move in and out of the lungs. This can result in a decrease in oxygen saturation and a rise in carbon dioxide levels in the blood, leading to respiratory failure in severe cases. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pneumonia: While patients with asthma may be at increased risk for developing pneumonia, the scenario does not provide any indication that the patient has an infection or signs of pneumonia on examination. Option B - Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening condition that can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough, but it is not a common complication of asthma and is unlikely to be the cause of the patient's symptoms based on the scenario. Option D - Bronchitis: Bronchitis is a respiratory condition that is characterized by inflammation of the bronchial tubes and can cause cough, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath. However, it is not the most likely complication of asthma in this scenario, as the patient's symptoms and signs are more consistent with an acute exacerbation of asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

He also reports palpitations. His vitals are: Temperature 97°F Blood pressure 130/80mmHg Pulse rate 108 beats per minute Respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute His thyroid gland is enlarged on examination, and his TSH level is low. Further investigations show elevated levels of T3 and T4. Which of the following is the appropriate staging system for the disease?
questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old female presents to the medical outpatient department complaining of swelling in the midline associated with cough and weight loss for the last five weeks. He also reports palpitations. His vitals are:
			Temperature 97°F
			Blood pressure 130/80mmHg
			Pulse rate 108 beats per minute
			Respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute
His thyroid gland is enlarged on examination, and his TSH level is low. Further investigations show elevated levels of T3 and T4. Which of the following is the appropriate staging system for the disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Burch-wartofsky scoring system: The clinical features of the case, as mentioned above, include an enlarged thyroid gland with low TSH . This is suggestive of hyperthyroidism . The Burch-Wartofsky scoring system is a clinical scoring system used to assess the severity of hyperthyroidism , particularly in the context of thyroid storms. The scoring system considers various clinical signs and symptoms, including temperature , heart rate , and central nervous system effects , to determine the severity of hyperthyroidism and guide treatment. The scoring system assigns points based on the following parameters: Body temperature: 0 points for < 37.2°C, 5 points for 37.2-37.7°C, 10 points for 37.8-38.2°C, 15 points for > 38.2°C. Central nervous system effects: 0 points for absent, 10 points for mild, and 20 points for severe. Gastrointestinal hepatic dysfunction: 0 points for absent, 10 points for mild, and 20 points for severe. Heart rate : 0 points for < 90 beats/min, 5 points for 90-109 beats/min, 10 points for 110-119 beats/min, and 15 points for > 119 beats/min. Congestive heart failure: 0 points for absence, 5 points for mild, 10 points for moderate, and 15 points for severe. The total score is then used to determine the severity of hyperthyroidism: Scores between 25-44 indicate mild to moderate hyperthyroidism Scores greater than 45 indicate severe hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm. The Burch-Wartofsky scoring system is useful in guiding treatment decisions for hyperthyroidism, particularly in the thyroid storm, and can help identify patients at higher risk of complications. However, it is important to note that the scoring system is not intended to replace clinical judgement or the individualized assessment of each patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - TNM staging: It is a staging system for various t umours, such as breast cancer. It does not apply to hyperthyroidism. Option B - Ann arbours staging: It is a staging system used for Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. It does not apply to hyperthyroidism. Option D - Child-pugh scoring system: It is a staging system used for cirrhosis and liver disease . It does not apply to hyperthyroidism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Renal failure: The adverse effect of acyclovir with the greatest morbidity is crystal-induced nephrotoxicity due to crystallization of the drug within the nephron. Acyclovir has low solubility in urine and therefore it is very important to ensure that patients are not intravascularly depleted as this complication of acyclovir therapy is much higher in patients that are volume contracted. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thrombocytopenia: Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count, which can result in an increased risk of bleeding. Acyclovir is not typically associated with thrombocytopenia as an adverse effect. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require close monitoring specifically for this drug. Option B - Liver Failure: Liver failure involves the severe impairment of liver function. Acyclovir is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, and significant liver toxicity is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy. While liver function tests might be monitored in some cases, liver failure is not a typical concern with acyclovir use. Option D - Pancytopenia : Pancytopenia refers to a decrease in all three major blood cell types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Acyclovir is not typically associated with pancytopenia. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require specific monitoring for this drug. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - It is an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor: Mycophenolate mofetil is an immunosuppressant agent used as a steroid sparing agent in many neurologic disorders, including neuromyelitis optica. It is a noncompetitive, reversible inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), an important enzyme in de novo purine synthesis. Guanosine monophosphate (the product of IMPDH acting on IMP) is not available in adequate amounts via the salvage pathway in lymphocytes. For this reason, the cytostatic effects of the drug are more lymphocyte selective (i.e., target tissue specific) than other steroid sparing agents. Option E - It is a DNA alkylating agent: it is the MOA of cyclophosphamide. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 56 years old female was diagnosed with COPD 4 years ago. At her regular maintenance visit she asks about pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV23). She has never undergone a surgical procedure, she doesn’t take steroids, and she smokes 1 ppd. She doesn’t remember if she ever received PPSV23. The MOST appropriate recommendation is:
questions.stemHtml: A 56 years old female was diagnosed with COPD 4 years ago. At her regular maintenance visit she asks about pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV23). She has never undergone a surgical procedure, she doesn’t take steroids, and she smokes 1 ppd. She doesn’t remember if she ever received PPSV23. The MOST appropriate recommendation is:

options.label: B
options.text: Delay PPSV23 until the age of 65

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe PPSV23 if she has frequent exacerbations

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe PPSV23 if she begins inhaled steroids

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Administer PPSV23 single dose: There are two types of pneumococcal vaccines: A pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23; Pneumovax 23, Pnu-Immune) and a pneumococcal protein-conjugate vaccine (PCV13; Prevnar 13). Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all adults ≥65 years old and adults <65 years old who are at risk for pneumococcal infection or severe complications from pneumococcal infection. The decision regarding whether both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated and whether revaccination with PPSV23 is indicated vary based on patient age and risk factors. For adults ages 19 to 64 years with certain chronic conditions (chronic heart, lung, or liver disease, diabetes mellitus, smoking, alcohol use disorder), a single dose of PPSV23 is recommended (which applies to this patient, and is the correct answer). For adults with higher risk conditions (immunocompromised state, asplenia, cerebrospinal fluid leak, cochlear implant, or history of invasive pneumococcal disease), both PCV13 and PPSV23 should be given. PCV13 in addition to PPSV23 is not recommended unless the patient has an indication for PCV13 (immunocompromised state, and the other already noted indications) because the incidence of pneumococcal disease caused by PCV13 serotypes is very low. If both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated PCV13 should be given before PPSV23, and they should be given at separate time points to help ensure that protective antibodies to each vaccine develop. If the primary indication for vaccination is age ≥65 years, PPSV23 should be given ≥1 year after PCV13. Most experts recommend revaccination with PPSV23 for selected patients because immunity to polysaccharide vaccines wanes over time, but recommendations on revaccination vary among experts and clinical practice guidelines. Incorrect Options: Option B - Delay PPSV23 until the age of 65: The patient already has a condition (COPD) that puts her at increased risk for pneumococcal disease, and her chronic smoking also contributes to her risk. The recommendation is to vaccinate adults between 19 to 64 years old with chronic conditions such as COPD with a single dose of PPSV23, regardless of their age. Waiting until the age of 65 could unnecessarily expose her to the risk of pneumococcal disease. Option C - Prescribe PPSV23 if she has frequent exacerbations: The presence of frequent exacerbations is not the deciding factor for pneumococcal vaccination. The vaccination should be administered based on the patient's age and underlying conditions, such as COPD, and not on the frequency of exacerbations. Waiting for exacerbations could unnecessarily delay the necessary immunization and expose her to the risk of pneumococcal disease. Option D - Prescribe PPSV23 if she begins inhaled steroids: The initiation of inhaled steroids is not a determining factor for pneumococcal vaccination. Although corticosteroids can increase the risk of infections, including pneumococcal disease, the decision to vaccinate against pneumococcus should be based on the patient's age and presence of conditions that increase her risk of pneumococcal disease, such as COPD, and not on her use of inhaled corticosteroids. In this patient's case, COPD itself is an indication for PPSV23 vaccination @Neet_pg_bot

What should you advise this patient regarding her ongoing medications?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Continue HCQ and prednisolone but she should stop MMF 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy: Your advice regarding ongoing medications should be to continue HCQ and prednisolone but she should stop MMF 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy. When planning pregnancy, it's important to consider the impact of medications on the developing fetus. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is generally considered safe during pregnancy and can be continued. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is contraindicated during pregnancy due to potential risks to the fetus. It should be discontinued at least 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy. Prednisolone is generally compatible with pregnancy and can be continued, although the dose might need to be adjusted based on the patient's condition and medical evaluation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Continue current medications: While the patient's medications need to be adjusted for pregnancy planning, simply continuing all current medications might not be the best approach, especially given the potential risks associated with certain medications during pregnancy. Option B - Continue HCQ and prednisolone but she should stop MMF 3 months before a planned pregnancy: The recommendation to stop mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) should be closer to 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy, as mentioned in the BSR and BHPR guidelines. Stopping MMF 3 months before may still expose the fetus to potential risks. Option D - Continue MMF and prednisolone but she should stop HCQ 6 weeks before a planned pregnancy: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is considered safe during pregnancy, and there's no need to discontinue it before a planned pregnancy. Stopping HCQ may result in a loss of disease control, which could be detrimental for the patient's health and pregnancy outcomes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman with endometriosis visited the doctor due to bilateral flank pain and decreased urine output for 1 week. Her abdomen has several surgical scars, as seen during a physical evaluation. According to laboratory tests, the blood creatinine level is 3.5 mg/dL. Numerous intra-abdominal adhesions are visible on an abdominal CT image, along with bilateral renal pelvis and proximal ureter enlargement. Which of the following is this patient's most probable underlying cause of renal dysfunction?

Her abdomen has several surgical scars, as seen during a physical evaluation. According to laboratory tests, the blood creatinine level is 3.5 mg/dL. Numerous intra-abdominal adhesions are visible on an abdominal CT image, along with bilateral renal pelvis and proximal ureter enlargement. options.label: C
options.text: Hydrostatic pressure in the efferent arteriole

options.label: D
options.text: Osmotic pressure in the afferent arteriole

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hydrostatic pressure in tubules: In this patient, bilateral occlusion of the urinary system due to post-surgical adhesions raises intraluminal ureteral pressure, which causes higher hydrostatic pressure in the renal tubules and Bowman capsule. This patient's increased serum creatinine indicates that the net glomerular filtration rate (GFR) has decreased because the glomerular hydrostatic pressure cannot compensate for the rise in the tubular hydrostatic pressure. The surrounding renal blood vessels may become compressed due to a prolonged increase in intratubular pressure, which may result in ischemic tubular atrophy, thinning of the renal cortex and medulla, and permanent loss of renal function. Incorrect Options: Option B - Osmotic pressure in glomeruli: Increased osmotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries would oppose the net flow of water across the capillary walls, reducing GFR. However, osmotically active solute content, unaffected by hydronephrosis, drives osmotic pressure in the glomeruli. As a result, this cannot be the main process causing renal dysfunction in hydronephrosis. Option C - Hydrostatic pressure in the efferent arteriole: The efferent arteriole's muscle tone is mainly responsible for hydrostatic pressure in the efferent arteriole (predominantly regulated by RAAS). Vasoconstriction of the efferent arterioles decreases renal plasma flow but boosts glomerular hydrostatic pressure, glomerular filtration rate, and filtration percentage. However, this patient's increased serum creatinine concentration points to renal dysfunction and a decreased glomerular filtration rate. Option D - Osmotic pressure in the afferent arteriole: The net flow of water across the capillary walls into the afferent arteriole would be reduced by a rise in osmotic pressure in the afferent arteriole. The Starling equation predicts that a rise in osmotic pressure in the sensory arteriole will result in a net reduction in GFR. However, given that the blood's solute concentration is unaffected, this is not the process causing the reduction in GFR associated with hydronephrosis. @Neet_pg_bot

On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the apex, which radiates to the axilla. Echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation with prolapse of the mitral valve leaflets. Which of the following structures prevents the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of shortness of breath and palpitations. He reports a past history of rheumatic fever during childhood. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the apex, which radiates to the axilla. Echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation with prolapse of the mitral valve leaflets. Which of the following structures prevents the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Chordae tendineae: The chordae tendineae are cord-like tendons that attach to the papillary muscles and the edges of the mitral and tricuspid valves in the heart. They play a crucial role in preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole. In mitral valve prolapse (MVP), the chordae tendineae may be elongated or ruptured , leading to the abnormal bulging of the mitral valve into the left atrium. This can result in mitral regurgitation, which can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath and palpitations, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B- Papillary muscles: The papillary muscles are small, cone-shaped muscles that are attached to the chordae tendineae and the ventricular walls. They contract during systole , pulling the chordae tendineae taut and preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium. However, in MVP, the papillary muscles are usually normal and the defect lies in the chordae tendineae. Option C- Tricuspid valve: The tricuspid valve is located between the right atrium and right ventricle , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. Option D- Aortic valve: The aortic valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Adenohypophysis: This patient's symptoms are consistent with a pituitary adenoma, which is most likely caused by abnormal growth of the adenohypophysis. Adenomas of the pituitary gland are usually due to proliferation of lactotroph cells, leading to hyperprolactinemia and suppression of gonadotropins causing secondary amenorrhea. Bitemporal hemianopsia and headaches may also develop due to compression of the optic chiasm as the adenoma grows. While a large non secreting pituitary adenoma could also explain her symptoms, the absence of other hypopituitarism symptoms makes prolactinoma more likely. Incorrect Options: Option A - Astrocytes: Astrocytomas are associated with rapidly progressive symptoms and typically occur in older individuals moreover this patient's symptoms, including secondary amenorrhea and bitemporal hemianopsia, are more indicative of a pituitary adenoma, which is caused by abnormal growth of cells in the adenohypophysis, not astrocytes. Arachnoid cap cells are a type of cells that make up the arachnoid villi, which play a role in the absorption of cerebrospinal fluid. Option D - Ependymal cells: Ependymomas, which are tumors that arise from ependymal cells, typically cause obstructive hydrocephalus, which can present as recurrent headaches. However, these tumours usually develop during childhood and are not associated with menstrual irregularities or visual disturbances Therefore, it is not likely that abnormal growth of ependymal cells is responsible for the patient's symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Absence of dopamine blockade of prolactin secretion
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Absence of dopamine blockade of prolactin secretion: Fluphenazine is a first-generation antipsychotic drug used to treat schizophrenia by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain. This reduces the activity of dopaminergic pathways involved in the symptoms of schizophrenia, including hallucinations and delusions. One of these pathways is the tuberoinfundibular pathway, which originates in the hypothalamus and inhibits prolactin release from the pituitary gland. Normally, dopamine binds to D2 receptors on lactotroph cells in the pituitary gland, reducing the sensitivity of these cells to prolactin-releasing hormones and inhibiting the release of prolactin. However, fluphenazine blocks D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, leading to decreased dopamine activity and increased prolactin secretion. This results in elevated levels of prolactin, which can cause a range of symptoms, including nipple discharge or galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and sexual dysfunction. Therefore, the mechanism responsible for the patient's symptoms of nipple discharge is the Absence of dopamine blockade of prolactin secretion in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. It is important to note that fluphenazine does not directly stimulate prolactin release. In reality, fluphenazine indirectly stimulates prolactin release by blocking dopamine receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, which removes the inhibition of prolactin release from the pituitary gland. Incorrect Options: Option B - Serotonin receptor antagonism: Serotonin receptor antagonism is not a mechanism involved in the development of nipple discharge. Fluphenazine is primarily a dopamine receptor antagonist, which blocks dopamine activity in the tuberoinfundibular pathway and leads to increased prolactin secretion. Although some atypical antipsychotic drugs have activity at serotonin receptors, this is not a mechanism relevant to the development of nipple discharge in this case. Option C - Direct prolactin release stimulation: Fluphenazine does not directly stimulate prolactin release from the pituitary gland. Instead, it blocks dopamine receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, removing the inhibition of prolactin release and increasing prolactin secretion. Option D - Histamine receptor antagonism: Histamine receptor antagonism is not a mechanism involved in developing nipple discharge. questions.stem: A leading nephrology institute researched the mechanism of action of a drug which causes hypokalemia and hypocalciuria. This particular drug acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.stemHtml: A leading nephrology institute researched the mechanism of action of a drug which causes hypokalemia and hypocalciuria. This particular drug acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Distal Tubules: The drug causing hypokalemia and hypocalciuria are likely Thiazide diuretic. Thiazide diuretic works on distal tubules of the kidney. The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) is a segment of the kidney's nephron located between the loop of Henle and the collecting duct. It regulates the number of electrolytes and water reabsorbed or excreted in the urine. The DCT is regulated by various hormones, including: Aldosterone , which stimulates sodium reabsorption. Atrial natriuretic peptide Angiotensin ll Parathyroid hormone Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) regulates water reabsorption. Thiazide diuretics act primarily on the early distal convoluted tubule (DCT) of the nephron in the kidney. They inhibit the Na+/Cl- co-transporter in the luminal membrane of the DCT, which reduces sodium and chloride reabsorption from the tubular fluid . It, in turn, increases the excretion of sodium, chloride, and water in the urine. Thiazide diuretics also decrease calcium reabsorption in the DCT, which can lead to a decrease in plasma calcium levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Proximal convoluted tubules: The proximal convoluted tubules (PCT) are a component of the nephrons in the kidneys responsible for the reabsorption of various substances from the filtrate produced by the glomerulus. The PCT is located in the cortex of the kidney and is the longest and most convoluted segment of the nephron. In the PCT, filtered substances such as glucose, amino acids, vitamins, and most electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, etc.) are reabsorbed into the bloodstream. Water is also reabsorbed in the PCT by osmosis, which helps to maintain the body's fluid balance. The hormone acting on proximal convoluted tubules includes: Angiotensin ll Parathyroid hormone Atrial natriuretic peptide The diuretics acting on PCT are as follows: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that works primarily in PCT. Mannitol affects the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) by increasing the osmotic pressure of the filtrate. Mannitol is commonly used to reduce intracranial pressure in patients with head injuries or brain tumours. Option B - Thick ascending loop of Henle: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is a segment of the nephron located in the renal medulla of the kidney. It plays a crucial role in urine formation by transporting sodium, potassium, and chloride ions out of the tubular fluid and into the interstitial fluid. The thick ascending limb is impervious to water, so it is not involved in reabsorption. The hormones acting on the thick ascending loop of Henle primarily include angiotensin-ll and aldosterone. The thick ascending limb is the site of action of loop diuretics, which are drugs that inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter. Loop diuretics reduce the reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride ions in the thick ascending limb, leading to increased excretion of these ions in the urine. It leads to hypokalemia, hyponatremia and hypercalciuria. Option D - Collecting tubules: The collecting tubules are the final segment of the nephron in the kidney. They receive filtrate from the distal convoluted tubule and are responsible for fine-tuning the final composition of urine before it is excreted from the body. The collecting tubules are divided into two types: The cortical collecting tubules The medullary collecting tubule s The hormones acting on collecting tubules are: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), or vasopressin, regulates water reabsorption. Aldosterone increases the reabsorption of sodium ions and the secretion of potassium ions. Potassium-sparing diuretics act on the collecting ducts of the nephron. These diuretics are called potassium-sparing because they reduce the excretion of potassium ions in urine , unlike loop and thiazide diuretics which increase potassium excretion. They work by blocking the action of aldosterone, increasing sodium and water excretion in urine, and reducing potassium loss. There are two main types of potassium-sparing diuretics: Aldosterone receptor antagonists e.g. spironolactone Sodium channel blockers , e.g. amiloride and triamterene. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: You are seeing a patient with advanced ER/PR+ Her2- breast cancer. Due to relapse with ddAC/T, she then was on SERD + CDK4/6 for 2 years, and then had progression. She has mild CKD, CTP A cirrhosis, diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension. Which of her comorbidities would disqualify her from a combination of ixabepilone + capecitabine?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cirrhosis The patient's cirrhosis, specifically Child-Pugh Class A, indicates a mild form of liver disease, which would impair the liver's ability to metabolize drugs like ixabepilone and capecitabine. This could lead to increased drug levels in the blood, causing a higher incidence of adverse effects, such as neutropenia-related sepsis. The liver's role in drug metabolism and the elevated risk of adverse effects in patients with liver disease make cirrhosis a contraindication for the use of ixabepilone + capecitabine. Incorrect Options: Option B - Diabetes: Diabetes does not generally contraindicate the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine. The metabolism and clearance of these drugs do not rely on insulin or glucose levels. However, diabetes might indirectly affect the patient's overall health and tolerance to treatment, so close monitoring would be needed. Option C - Hypertension: While hypertension should be well-controlled before initiating any chemotherapy due to potential cardiovascular risk, it is not a specific contraindication for the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine. Option D - CKD (Chronic Kidney Disease): Mild CKD does not contraindicate the use of ixabepilone and capecitabine, as these drugs are primarily metabolized in the liver. However, in severe renal impairment, capecitabine use should be avoided due to an increased risk of adverse reactions. As this patient has only mild CKD, it is not a contraindication for this combination therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Dexamethasone 4 mg IV q 6 hours : This is the appropriate course of action. The patient's presentation with metastatic prostate cancer and symptoms of back pain, muscle weakness, and decreased sensation in the bilateral legs is highly concerning for spinal cord compression, which is considered an oncologic emergency. The immediate treatment of choice is dexamethasone to reduce spinal cord inflammation and edema, thus relieving compression. Patients with clinical symptoms suggestive of spinal cord compression should receive an urgent MRI of the entire spine to confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the compression. However, the initiation of steroids should not be delayed pending imaging. Incorrect Options: Option A- CT guided biopsy of the disease in the T-spine : Performing a biopsy is not the immediate course of action in this emergent situation. The priority is to relieve the spinal cord compression and address the patient's symptoms. A biopsy may be considered later to determine the nature of the spinal lesion, but it should not delay treatment. Option B- Dexamethasone 2 mg IV q 12 hours : While dexamethasone is the correct choice, a dose of 2 mg every 12 hours may be insufficient in this acute situation. The patient should receive a higher initial dose (commonly 4 mg every 6 hours) to adequately address spinal cord inflammation and edema. Option D- Docetaxel chemotherapy with a plan for 6 cycles : Initiating chemotherapy is not the immediate priority in a patient with spinal cord compression. The patient requires urgent management of the spinal cord compression to prevent further neurological deficits and address pain and symptoms. questions.stem: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized for longer than anticipated due to decreased kidney function. The patient claims that his symptoms have improved considerably since then. He is now urinating considerably more than he was before the procedure. His serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, and his blood urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Hypokalemia About two weeks after the initial event, acute kidney injury (AKI) patients typically recover full glomerular filtration function. However, tubular reabsorption is still impaired, leading to increased urine production and subsequent polyuria. Several electrolytes, such as potassium, sodium, and magnesium, that are typically reabsorbed by the tubules, are lost during the polyuric recovery period of AKI. Incorrect options: Option B: Hypernatremia This patient is in the polyuric recovery stage of AKI three weeks after exposure to contrast and is more at risk for hyponatremia than hypernatremia. Patients experience several electrolyte losses during this time, including sodium, which is typically reabsorbed by the tubules. Option C: Hyporeninemia Patients with AKI in the polyuric recovery phase are at risk for volume depletion, characterized by a decline in GFR and salt delivery to the distal nephrons and the subsequent release of renin. As a result, this patient would produce more renin. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis This patient's polyuric recovery phase of AKI has been present for three weeks following contrast exposure. Patients are at risk for metabolic acidosis rather than alkalosis during this time because they cannot excrete H+ ions and regenerate bicarbonate (both functions of the tubule system). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Flattening of the optic chiasm: Several findings on head MRI can help establish the diagnosis of intracranial hypotension. These include diffuse, non-nodular enhancement of the pachymeninges (without leptomeningeal enhancement); “sagging of the brain” which can result in descent of the cerebellar tonsils, flattening of the anterior pons, obliteration of the basal cisterns and flattening of the optic chiasm; subdural fluid collections; enlargement of the pituitary which can mimic pituitary tumor; engorgement of the cerebral venous sinuses; and decrease in the size of the ventricles. Incorrect Options: Option A - Leptomeningeal Enhancement: Leptomeningeal enhancement refers to the abnormal enhancement of the meninges (the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord) on imaging studies, typically seen as bright areas on contrast-enhanced MRI. While leptomeningeal enhancement can occur in various conditions, such as infections, inflammation, and certain cancers, it is not a specific finding that suggests spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH). Option B - Enlargement of the Basal Cisterns: Enlargement of the basal cisterns is not a typical finding in spontaneous intracranial hypotension. In fact, SIH is characterized by the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to decreased CSF pressure and resultant brain sagging rather than enlargement of the basal cisterns. Option D - Flattening of the Pituitary: Flattening of the pituitary gland may be seen in cases of intracranial hypotension, but it is not as specific or characteristic as other findings. Spontaneous intracranial hypotension can lead to changes in brain structures, including the downward displacement of the brain ("brain sagging"), which can affect the pituitary gland's position. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.solution: Option C- Proximal tubule: The kidneys play a key role in regulating the acid-base balance of the body by removing excess acid or base from the blood. The proximal tubule is the primary site of acid-base regulation in the kidney, where bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) are reabsorbed from the filtrate and returned to the bloodstream. Bicarbonate ions are important for buffering acids in the blood and maintaining a pH that is compatible with normal bodily functions. When there is an excess of acid in the blood, such as in the case of respiratory acidosis, the kidneys respond by increasing the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions in the proximal tubule, which helps to neutralise the excess acid and restore the acid-base balance of the body. This process is regulated by several mechanisms, including the action of carbonic anhydrase enzymes in the proximal tubule, which catalyse the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) into carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions (H+). The hydrogen ions are secreted into the filtrate in exchange for the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions, which are then returned to the bloodstream to help buffer excess acid. Therefore, option C is correct because the proximal tubule is responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Incorrect Options: Option A- Glomerulus: The glomerulus is responsible for filtering blood and removing waste products from the bloodstream, but it is not directly involved in regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The glomerulus is a network of capillaries in the renal corpuscle that is responsible for filtering blood and producing a filtrate that contains water, electrolytes, and waste products. The filtrate produced by the glomerulus is then modified as it passes through the renal tubules, where various substances are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream or secreted into the urine. While the glomerulus is not directly involved in acid-base regulation, it does play a role in maintaining the electrolyte balance of the body by filtering out excess sodium and other electrolytes from the blood. Therefore, option A is incorrect because the glomerulus is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option B- Bowman's capsule: Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus in the renal corpuscle and collects the filtrate that is produced by the glomerulus. While Bowman's capsule is involved in the initial filtration of blood in the kidney, it is not directly involved in the regulation of acid-base balance. Once the filtrate is collected in Bowman's capsule, it then passes into the renal tubules where it is modified and processed. Therefore, option B is incorrect because Bowman's capsule is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option D- Distal tubule: The distal tubule is a part of the renal tubule that comes after the loop of Henle and is responsible for fine-tuning the concentration of urine by reabsorbing some ions and water and secreting others. While the distal tubule plays a role in regulating the balance of electrolytes in the body, it is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The distal tubule does have some capacity to regulate acid-base balance, but its primary function is the regulation of salt and water balance in the body. Therefore, option D is incorrect because the distal tubule is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

MRI of the liver is a non-invasive method used to assess the degree of systemic iron deposition in patients with thalassemia. Elevated serum ferritin levels suggest iron overload, and MRI can provide valuable information about iron concentration within the liver. Monitoring for iron overload is important to prevent potential complications associated with excess iron accumulation, including liver damage. Option C - Liver biopsy: A liver biopsy could be used to diagnose iron overload, but it's invasive and not necessary when other non-invasive methods are available. questions.stem: A 54-year-old male presents to the medical emergency department complaining of watery diarrhoea and profuse sweating for the last 12 hours. He reports having had bowel disease over the previous four years. Further evaluation confirms a history of Crohn's disease. He says he has had 8 to 10 episodes of watery diarrhoea since last night. His ECG shows flat T waves and the appearance of U waves. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals alkalosis. What is the most likely metabolic disorder here?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old male presents to the medical emergency department complaining of watery diarrhoea and profuse sweating for the last 12 hours. He reports having had bowel disease over the previous four years. Further evaluation confirms a history of Crohn's disease. He says he has had 8 to 10 episodes of watery diarrhoea since last night. His ECG shows flat T waves and the appearance of U waves. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals alkalosis. What is the most likely metabolic disorder here?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Hypokalemia: The clinical features of watery diarrhoea secondary to Crohn's disease and the appearance of U waves and flat T waves suggest hypokalemia to be the likely metabolic disorder. Hypokalemia (less than three mEq/L or three mmol/L) is a decrease in the serum potassium level. The normal potassium level is 3.5 to 5 mEq/L. Causes of hypokalemia with alkalosis: Vomiting Thiazide and loop diuretics Cushing's syndrome Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) Causes of hypokalemia with acidosis: Diarrhoea Renal tubular acidosis Acetazolamide Partially treated diabetic ketoacidosis Magnesium deficiency may also cause hypokalemia. The investigation includes serum potassium and magnesium levels. ECG changes include: U waves Flat T waves (occasionally inversion) Prolong PR interval ST depression Management includes oral or intravenous potassium administration. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypercalcemia: Hypercalcemia is a raised calcium level and can present with kidney stones, bone pains, and muscle weakness. A short QT interval resulting from a short ST segment is the most frequent ECG finding in hypercalcemia. Option B- Hyponatremia: Hyponatremia is a sodium level of less than 135 mmol/L. There is low plasma and urine osmolality but no ECG changes. So it is less likely in the case mentioned above. questions.solution: Correct Option B - A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. questions.stem: A 45-year-old blind patient seeks medical attention for long-standing sleep problems. He has been completely blind since age 32. For the past 10 years, he has suffered from periods of nocturnal insomnia and daytime sleepiness which are very disruptive to his work and family life. In between these periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness, he may have weeks of near-normal night-time sleep. A 14-day actigraphy record shows a daily delay drift of the onset and offset of the sleep-wake rhythm with a circadian period that is longer than 24 hours. Which of the following medications is preferred in the treatment of this disorder?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old blind patient seeks medical attention for long-standing sleep problems. He has been completely blind since age 32. For the past 10 years, he has suffered from periods of nocturnal insomnia and daytime sleepiness which are very disruptive to his work and family life. In between these periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness, he may have weeks of near-normal night-time sleep. A 14-day actigraphy record shows a daily delay drift of the onset and offset of the sleep-wake rhythm with a circadian period that is longer than 24 hours. Which of the following medications is preferred in the treatment of this disorder?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Melatonin: The clinical scenario described is consistent with non-24-hour sleep wake disorder (N24SWD). In blind patients the mainstay of treatment for N24SWD is melatonin combined with structured behavioral cues such as regular timing of meals, and physical activity. In individuals with some residual light perception, bright light in the morning shortly after awakening can be added to the above measures. Incorrect Options: Option B - Zolpidem: Zolpidem is a sedative-hypnotic medication used to treat insomnia. It acts on the GABA receptors to promote sleep initiation. While it may help improve sleep onset and maintenance in some individuals, it does not address the underlying circadian rhythm disruption seen in the blind patient with irregular sleep patterns. Option C - Eszopiclone: Eszopiclone is another sedative-hypnotic medication indicated for treating insomnia. Similar to zolpidem, it primarily targets sleep initiation and maintenance rather than addressing circadian rhythm disturbances. Option D - Modafinil: Modafinil is a wakefulness-promoting agent used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness, such as that seen in narcolepsy or shift work sleep disorder. It is not typically used to address the circadian rhythm disruption and irregular sleep-wake patterns observed in blind individuals. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Infrarenal abdominal aorta: An aortic aneurysm is defined as the dilation of the aortic lumen. The most common site of an aortic aneurysm is the infrarenal abdominal aorta. The shape of the aneurysm is fusiform or saccular, which helps to differentiate it from a false aneurysm . Abdominal aortic aneurysms affect males more commonly than females. It occurs in about 5% of men who are over the age of 60 years. Incorrect Options: Option B- Suprarenal abdominal aorta: An aortic aneurysm can occur above the kidneys and is called a suprarenal aortic aneurysm. A suprarenal aortic aneurysm can affect 10-20% of patients . A suprarenal aortic aneurysm is less common than an infrarenal aortic aneurysm. Option C- Descending thoracic aorta: Aneurysmal dilation of the variable length of the descending aorta can occur in some patients. It can occur in 10-20% of patients with aortic aneurysms. It is not as common as an infrarenal aortic aneurysm. Option D- Ascending thoracic aorta: Aortic aneurysm does not occur commonly in the ascending thoracic aorta. The ascending thoracic aorta is usually spared, and aneurysmal dilation does not occur at this location @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A medical student in the beginning of 3rd year comes to your office with a complaint of excessive tiredness. She is having trouble concentrating and finds herself dozing off in lectures and during morning rounds. She has always been a “night owl”. In college, she took all afternoon classes so she could sleep in. She would go to bed at 2 AM and get up at 10 or 11 AM and had no trouble falling asleep or staying awake during the day. In the first 2 years of medical school, she skipped all morning lectures. However, as a third year, she has to be in the hospital no later than 7 AM to pre-round her patients. She tries to go to bed at 9:00 PM, but lies awake in bed until the middle of the night despite being “exhausted.” She has trouble getting up at 5:30 AM when her alarm goes off. On her days off, she goes to sleep when she’s tired, usually “pretty late,” falls asleep easily, and then sleeps in, sometimes until the afternoon. Her partner says she does not snore or wake up gasping. She has not experienced any episodes of muscle weakness or paralysis. She admits that she is stressed but not more than usual. She drinks socially but denies any illicit drug use. She drinks several cups of coffee throughout the morning but not after 2 PM. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder This patient reports a chronic inability to fall asleep and wake up at socially acceptable times which is consistent with a circadian rhythm disorder. When she was allowed to sleep and wake up at her preferred time (for example when she was in college) her sleep and daytime function were normal. However, now that she has to wake up early in the morning she has difficulty shifting her bedtime to earlier in the night which results in insufficient sleep and daytime sleepiness. This is consistent with delayed sleep-phase disorder (DSPD). Patients with DSPD typically fall asleep between 1 AM and 6 AM and wake up in the late morning or early afternoon. They often struggle with decreased academic performance, especially during morning hours, in addition to tardiness and absenteeism. Treatment with bright light in the morning has been shown to successfully advance circadian rhythms in patients with this condition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Obstructive sleep apnea: This patient lacks typical signs and symptoms of sleep apnea (snoring, gasping, and morning headaches) and her sleep is refreshing when she goes to bed and wakes up later in the day. Option B - Sleep Onset Insomnia: Sleep onset insomnia is characterized by chronic difficulty falling asleep resulting in daytime impairment. This patient has no trouble falling asleep or staying asleep when she is allowed to go to bed and wake up at her preferred bedtime and only struggles when she has to stick to an earlier schedule which is typical of delayed sleep-phase disorder. Option C - Behaviorally-induced insufficient sleep syndrome: This is a voluntary restriction of sleep (for example by staying up late to study or working two jobs) that leads to sleep deprivation, excessive daytime sleepiness, and a decreased level of alertness. questions.stem: A 32-year-old female, Rh negative, after an RTA had required more than 20 units of blood. She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female, Rh negative, after an RTA had required more than 20 units of blood. She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?

options.label: A
options.text: Check serum for anti-IgG Rh anti-body

options.label: B
options.text: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm the Rh status of the partner

questions.answerText: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin: In Rh-negative women who have been exposed to Rh-positive blood, such as through transfusion or pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, there is a risk of developing Rh sensitization. Rh sensitization can lead to the production of antibodies against Rh-positive blood, which can be a significant concern in future pregnancies. To prevent this, a dose of anti-Rh immunoglobulin (Rhogam) is administered to the Rh-negative woman. This immunoglobulin binds to any Rh-positive blood cells that might have entered her bloodstream, preventing her immune system from reacting to them and thus reducing the risk of sensitization. This is particularly important when the woman is planning future pregnancies with an Rh-positive partner to prevent the development of HDN in the newborn. Incorrect Options: Option A - Check serum for anti-IgG Rh anti-body: Checking serum for anti-IgG Rh antibody is not the ideal approach in this situation. The goal is to prevent Rh sensitization, and waiting for the development of antibodies could lead to complications in future pregnancies. Option C - Confirm the Rh status of the partner: Confirming the Rh status of the partner is important, but regardless of the partner's Rh status, if the woman is Rh-negative and has been exposed to Rh-positive blood, administration of anti-Rh immunoglobulin is recommended to prevent sensitization. Option D - No further intervention: No further intervention is not appropriate in this case. Rh sensitization can lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in future pregnancies, which can cause severe anemia and other complications in the baby. @Neet_pg_bot

Investigations reveal positive anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies. Which of the following is the most effective treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents to the medical outpatient department with a midline neck swelling for 1 month. Physical examination reveals a rubbery and mobile goitre. Investigations reveal positive anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies. Which of the following is the most effective treatment for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Levothyroxine: The patient presents with the clinical features and investigative findings of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. The patients usually present with signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism , including weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, lethargy, slowness of movements, dry skin, hair loss, menorrhagia, hoarseness, depression, infertility, myalgias and a goitre. The goitre is a small to moderately sized diffuse, which may be firm or rubbery in consistency. Laboratory investigations reveal high TSH and low to normal T4 levels . Anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies are present in more than 90% of the patients . Treatment includes levothyroxine, as the patients are usually in a hypothyroid state. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies: The child is suffering from meningitis. questions.solution: Correct Option C - 5 mm: The cutoff value to start prophylaxis for latent tuberculosis in HIV patients is to have indurated area of atleast 5mm on the Mantoux test. Latent tuberculosis: Tuberculosis (TB) caused by bacteria of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex affects the lungs, but other organs may be involved in up to one-third of cases. Transmission usually occurs through the airborne spread of droplet nuclei produced by patients with infectious pulmonary TB. The risk of developing disease depends on the host defense mechanisms. The key to the diagnosis of TB is a high index of suspicion. Patient screening for latent TB infection can be done using Mantoux test of interferon gamma release assay. However, these tests cannot differentiate between active and latent infection and have low predictive value in identifying patients with a higher risk of developing an active infection. TST cutoff points are largely related to the probability of a true infection and the likelihood of developing TB if truly infected. The cutoff point is usually set at 10 mm for mildly-at-risk patients, while those with very low risk are set at 15 mm. HIV-infected persons, close contacts with infected individuals, immunosuppressed patients, and those with fibrotic lesions on imaging consistent with old TB have lower cutoff points (5mm). options.label: A
options.text: Albumin and prealbumin are the best measures of nutritional status in critically ill patients

options.label: B
options.text: Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients

options.label: C
options.text: Healthy patients have a daily protein requirement of 1.8 g/kg/day actual body weight

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients: Although a short period of nutritional deprivation may be tolerated, physiologic function and nutritional status are affected by significant deprivation over 1-2 weeks. Factors that influence the need for nutritional supplementation include pre-illness status and severity and duration of metabolic stress. In critically ill patients, nutritional support should be initiated relatively as early as 24-48 hours after admission, as it may improve outcomes. If oral intake cannot maintain adequate nutritional intake, enteral or intravenous routes should be considered. Enteral nutrition is preferable when it is tolerated. Patients who will require 7 days or more of nutrition support should be considered for parenteral nutrition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Albumin and prealbumin are the best measures of nutritional status in critically ill patients: Albumin and prealbumin are acute phase reactants and may be falsely elevated in critically ill patients. Option C - Healthy patients have a daily protein requirement of 1.8 g/kg/day actual body weight : The protein requirement for a healthy patient is 0.8 g/kg/day actual body weight. Option D - The absence of bowel sounds is a contraindication to enteral feeding : The only contraindication to enteral feeding is high bowel obstruction. Lack of bowel sounds or lack of flatus are not contraindications to enteral feeding. @Neet_pg_bot

She has an allergy to penicillin with documented anaphylaxis. History is notable for exposure to an outdoor dog. She lives in a wooded area and denies known tick bites. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Doxycycline: This patient is pregnant and PCN allergic with neurologic manifestations of lyme disease and she likely has early disseminated Lyme disease. The treatments of choice in non-pregnant patients in this setting are doxycycline and ceftriaxone (particularly if the lumbar puncture was positive for meningitis or if there was neurological involvement other than Bell’s palsy). Although tetracyclines are generally avoided in pregnancy, doxycycline rather than a second-line agent (eg, azithromycin) has been shown to be safe when a short course is required. The risk of hepatotoxicity in the mother and adverse effects on fetal bone and teeth associated with many tetracyclines are extremely rare with doxycycline. Option B - Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is not a standard treatment for Lyme disease. Option D - Azithromycin: Although azithromycin is an acceptable 2nd line choice in some situations, it would not be a good choice in the setting of neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with complaints of decreased consciousness level. There is no history of fever or headaches in the past. During the examination, it is found that the patient has a temperature of 95°F, a blood pressure of 60/40 mmHg, a pulse rate of 46 beats per minute, and a blood sugar level of 64 mg/dl. Apart from the delayed relaxation of the ankle reflex, there is no focused neurological. Serum TSH level is 100 mU/L. Which of the subsequent diagnoses is the most likely possibility here?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with complaints of decreased consciousness level. There is no history of fever or headaches in the past. During the examination, it is found that the patient has a temperature of 95°F, a blood pressure of 60/40 mmHg, a pulse rate of 46 beats per minute, and a blood sugar level of 64 mg/dl. Apart from the delayed relaxation of the ankle reflex, there is no focused neurological. Serum TSH level is 100 mU/L. Which of the subsequent diagnoses is the most likely possibility here?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Myxedema coma: Clinical features like depressed consciousness, bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycemia in a 70-year-old patient with a very high TSH level are very suggestive of Myxedema coma. It is profound hypothyroidism commonly seen in the elderly and usually precipitated by different medical conditions. Myxedema coma is a rare and life-threatening complication of severe, untreated hypothyroidism. Precipitating factors of myxedema coma include: Medications: Withdrawal of thyroxin Infections Burns Myocardial infarction Stroke Surgery Diagnosis: Low body temperature and poor mental condition are two clinical signs of myxedema coma. Low blood pressure Low blood sugar Hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypernatremia, and sluggish heartbeat. In the winter, when hypothermia is more prevalent, myxedema coma is most common in adults 60 years of age and older. Myxedema coma is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment in the hospital, including intravenous thyroid hormone replacement therapy and supportive care to stabilize the patient's vital signs and prevent complications. Incorrect Options: Option A - Addison's disease: Although clinical features described in the above scenario are also seen in Addison's disease but raised, TSH is not a feature of Addison's disease. Addison's disease is a rare autoimmune disorder in which the adrenal glands do not produce enough cortisol and aldosterone hormones . This leads to a range of symptoms, including fatigue, weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, and darkening of the skin. Addison's disease can also cause a life-threatening condition called an adrenal crisis, which can result in shock and multiple organ failure. Option C - Hyperthyroidism: Above mention, signs and symptoms are not due to hyperthyroidism and in hyperthyroidism, TSH is decreased, not increased. Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland produces an excess of thyroid hormones. This leads to an increase in metabolic rate, causing symptoms such as weight loss, rapid heartbeat, anxiety, and tremors. In severe cases, hyperthyroidism can lead to a life-threatening condition called thyroid storm , which can cause fever, delirium, rapid heart rate, and organ failure. Option D - Septic shock: Although clinical features of septic shock and myxedema coma overlap, it is not associated with raised TSH levels . Secondly, septic shock is associated with warm peripheries. Septic shock is a severe systemic infection that can cause widespread inflammation throughout the body, leading to a range of symptoms such as fever, rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, and organ failure . Septic shock is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment , including antibiotics and intravenous fluids, to control the infection and stabilize the patient's vital signs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: This patient presents with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina. Indications of CABG are as follows: High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization Post Infarct angina Indications for emergency CABG Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG. Option C- Thrombolytic therapy: Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle. Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI. These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy. @Neet_pg_bot
