questions.stem: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - High cortisol and low ACTH: Cushing syndrome involves the excess of all adrenal hormones. It is diagnosed by: Demonstration of high cortisol level Serum ACTH levels Dexamethasone suppression test Salivary cortisol 24-hour urinary-free cortisol Radiologic imaging. The outpatient initial screening test is 24-hour urinary-free cortisol. The best initial diagnostic test is an overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by a 1 mg loading dose. To localise the lesion, a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is carried out to differentiate between pituitary adenoma and ectopic source. If ACTH is low and cortisol is high, there is either an adrenal adenoma or exogenous glucocorticoid intake. However, if ACTH is high and cortisol is low, then there is either pituitary adenoma or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. If the cortisol levels are suppressed, followed by a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, the cause is a pituitary adenoma. Contrarily, if no suppression has occurred, the cause is an ectopic source of ACTH. Incorrect Options: Option B - High cortisol and high ACTH: If ACTH is high and cortisol is also high, there is either pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease) or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. Option C - Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia: In Cushing syndrome, there is an excess aldosterone secretion that results in hypernatremia and hypokalemia. Option D - Decreased urinary free cortisol: Increased urinary-free cortisol is present in Cushing syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension. His current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and amlodipine. His latest laboratory results show an elevated serum potassium level of 5.5 mEq/L. The nephrologist decides to modify his medication regimen to manage his CKD and hyperkalemia. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension. His current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and amlodipine. His latest laboratory results show an elevated serum potassium level of 5.5 mEq/L. The nephrologist decides to modify his medication regimen to manage his CKD and hyperkalemia. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. Incorrect options: Option B: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option C: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic medication that can also reduce blood pressure in patients with CKD. It has no effect on reducing proteinuria. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Elevated hemoglobin A1c levels: While hyperglycemia at the time of the gastric emptying study can be associated with delayed gastric emptying and a false-positive gastric emptying study, a history of diabetes or an elevated hemoglobin A1c level with a normal blood glucose at the time of the study will not be associated with a false-positive test. Anticholinergic agents such as benztropine will also be associated with a false-positive study. However, domperidone, which is used to stimulate gastric motility (but is not approved for use in the United States), can lead to a false-negative gastric emptying study. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia refers to high blood sugar levels, which can be associated with diabetes. While uncontrolled diabetes can lead to various complications, including gastrointestinal issues, it does not directly impact the results of a gastric emptying study. Hyperglycemia might exacerbate certain gastrointestinal symptoms, but it would not cause false-positive or false-negative results in the study. Option C - Domperidone: Domperidone is a medication used to treat nausea and vomiting. It works by increasing the movement or contractions of the stomach and intestines. If someone is taking domperidone during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results by affecting gastric motility. It could lead to false-negative results, where the study may show normal or faster gastric emptying due to the effects of the medication. Option D - Benztropine: Benztropine is an anticholinergic medication used to treat certain movement disorders and side effects of antipsychotic medications. It works by blocking the action of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter in the nervous system. Anticholinergic drugs can slow down gastrointestinal motility, which could lead to delayed gastric emptying. Therefore, if someone is taking benztropine during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results and cause false-positive results, indicating delayed gastric emptying when it's primarily due to the medication's effects. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Oligoprogression refers to the clinical scenario where a few metastases progress, whereas all other metastases are stable or responding to a systemic therapy strategy.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Oligoprogression refers to the clinical scenario where a few metastases progress, whereas all other metastases are stable or responding to a systemic therapy strategy The oligoprogressive phase is a relapsed phase of oligometastatic cancer after a cytoreductive treatment. questions.stem: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Prophylactic anticoagulation: This patient with acute onset left-sided weakness and aphasia is most likely suffering from a stroke, particularly an embolic stroke in light of this patient’s underlying atrial fibrillation as proven by the ECG findings. Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria. Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region. The risk of thrombosis can be reduced by the use of anticoagulation that prevents the formation of clots that eventually lodge in the distal circulation. Incorrect Options: Option A- Synchronized cardioversion: This treatment modality is used to terminate atrial fibrillation that leads to hemodynamic instability i.e. hypotension. It cannot mitigate the risk of thrombosis. Option C- Defibrillation: This intervention is used to terminate ventricular fibrillation It has no role in A-fib Option D- Angioplasty: Angioplasty is done in cases of myocardial infarction which presents as chest pain radiating to the neck and left arm, diaphoresis, and an impending sense of doom. An MI presents with ST-elevations on ECG @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Fusobacterium nucleatum: The most common anaerobic species in pulmonary empyemas was found to be Fusobacterium nucleatum, which are small spindle shaped organisms frequently present in gum disease and contributes to dental plaque formation. The organism is known for its characteristic to adhere to both type IV collagen and other microorganisms, and is the most likely oral bacterium to be involved in infections in distant sites of the body. Incorrect Options: Option A - Microaerophilic streptococci: Though slightly less common than fusobacterium, is a frequent pathogen involved in parapneumonic effusions and empyemas and more often than not is a component of a polymicrobial infection with anaerobes and aerobes. Option C - Prevotella: Is a non-motile, anaerobic, gram negative rod which is part of the normal flora of the mouth and is involved in gingival disease. The species has the propensity to cause infections at distant sites of the body, especially the lungs through aspiration. Option D - Bacteroides species: Are anaerobic gram negative rods, and are a component of the normal flora of the gut. They have the potential to cause abscesses throughout the body. The most common species encountered in the laboratory is B. fragilis, which are susceptible to carbapenems and metronidazole yet have a high rate of resistance to penicillin, cefoxitin, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Faint band in the hemoglobin A region after 2 units of red blood cell transfusions given 2 months ago: While it is possible to observe a faint band in the hemoglobin A region after recent blood transfusions due to the presence of donor red blood cells (which contain hemoglobin A), the lifespan of transfused red blood cells is much shorter than 60 days (approximately 7-10 days). Therefore, seeing a faint band 2 months after transfusion is unusual. Option D - The presence of fetal hemoglobin, alpha-2 gamma-2: Patients with beta thalassemia major often have increased levels of fetal hemoglobin (Hb F), which is composed of alpha-2 and gamma-2 globin chains. The presence of Hb F is a characteristic feature of beta thalassemia major. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - ACTH assay interference: In an SST, blood is first collected for baseline measurement of plasma cortisol and ACTH level. Then, 250 µg of Synacthen is administered intramuscularly, followed by measurement of cortisol levels at 30 and/or 60 minutes post-Synacthen. The cut-off for a normal cortisol response must be laboratory-specific or assay-specific (ranging from 420 to 574 nmol/L) due to variations among different cortisol assays. In this case, given the high plasma ACTH and borderline low cortisol levels, a short synacthen test (SST) was ordered, which showed normal serum cortisol levels post-Synacthen i.e. >550nmol/L, thereby excluding adrenal insufficiency. In cases of recent onset of secondary adrenal failure up to 4 weeks, it may produce a normal response to an SST but with low ACTH levels. However, in this case, the plasma ACTH that was repeated as part of the SST remained elevated at 40 pmol/L. This discordance between plasma ACTH and SST results should raise suspicion of ACTH assay interference. Measurement of plasma ACTH is an important step in determining the underlying cause of hypercortisolemia. Interfering substances in the immunoassays can lead to erroneous results impacting clinical management and leading to unnecessary investigations and interventions. questions.stem: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Anti-muscle-specific kinase antibodies: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the most common antibodies found in patients with myasthenia gravis. These antibodies are present in nearly 95% of patients diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Other groups of patients with significantly higher involvement of bulbar muscles have muscle-specific kinase antibodies. These antibodies occur in nearly 50% of patients with myasthenia gravis. They are produced against the phosphorylating enzyme in the skeletal muscles. Their role is defined in patients with bulbar involvement or in patients seronegative for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The sensitivity is in the following order: acetylcholine receptor (postsynaptic) > muscle-specific kinase antibodies. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (pre-synaptic): Unlike Lambert-Eaton syndrome where the antibodies are against presynaptic calcium channels, myasthenia is primarily a postsynaptic disorder. Antibodies are produced against postsynaptic receptors or muscle-specific kinase. This describes the presynaptic antibody, which is not related to myasthenia. Option B - Anti-acetylcholinesterase antibodies: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme that metabolizes the acetylcholine released in the synaptic cleft. Destruction of this enzyme would produce symptoms similar to organophosphate poisoning. This would lead to increased activity of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Myasthenia is primarily a disease of nicotinic receptors, and these antibodies have no relation to myasthenia gravis. Option D - Anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies: Patients with thymoma have a high incidence of myasthenia gravis. This has been attributed to a T-cell-mediated autoimmune response observed in patients with hyperactive thymus. This, however, is not related to anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies. These antibodies are therapeutically used in patients who receive transplanted organs and are used for immunosuppression. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old previously healthy male is admitted with florid diarrhea for 3 days. He was treated with clindamycin 2 weeks ago for a dental abscess. He is afebrile with the following vital signs: HR 98, RR 16, saturation on room air 98%, and BP 110/86. The exam is only notable for mild abdominal tenderness. C. diff toxin and Ag are positive, and he is started on metronidazole treatment. Which of the following precautions must be taken to prevent the spread of Clostridium difficile infection in the hospital? I. Wash hands with soap and water before and after seeing the patient. II. Use bleach to clean the equipment and room. III. Use antiseptic hand spray when entering and leaving the room (no need to wash hands). IV. Use airborne precautions. V. Use gloves and a gown when entering the room.
questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old previously healthy male is admitted with florid diarrhea for 3 days. He was treated with clindamycin 2 weeks ago for a dental abscess. He is afebrile with the following vital signs: HR 98, RR 16, saturation on room air 98%, and BP 110/86. The exam is only notable for mild abdominal tenderness. C. diff toxin and Ag are positive, and he is started on metronidazole treatment. Which of the following precautions must be taken to prevent the spread of Clostridium difficile infection in the hospital?
I. Wash hands with soap and water before and after seeing the patient.
II. Use bleach to clean the equipment and room.
III. Use antiseptic hand spray when entering and leaving the room (no need to wash hands).
IV. Use airborne precautions.
V. Use gloves and a gown when entering the room.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - I, II, and V: Hand hygiene is the single most important prevention for nosocomial infection. When entering a room of a patient with C. difficile infection, all personnel (health care workers as well as visitors) should wear gloves and gowns. To prevent the spread of Clostridium difficile infection in the hospital, the following precautions should be taken: I. Wash hands with soap and water before and after seeing the patient. Hand hygiene with soap and water is essential because alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against C. difficile spores. II. Use bleach to clean the equipment and room. Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) is effective in killing C. difficile spores and preventing transmission. V. Use gloves and a gown when entering the room. Healthcare workers should wear gloves and a gown when entering the room of a patient with C. difficile infection to prevent contamination of their hands and clothing. Incorrect Options: Option A - I and III: Regular antiseptic is not effective in getting rid of spores, so handwashing with soap and water is essential. Option C - I–V: Airborne precautions are not required. Option D - II, III, and V: Chlorine-containing cleaning agents or sporicidal agents should be used to clean the room and equipment. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option B - I, II, and V:

Hand hygiene is the single most important prevention for nosocomial infection. When entering a room of a patient with C. difficile infection, all personnel (health care workers as well as visitors) should wear gloves and gowns.

To prevent the spread of Clostridium difficile infection in the hospital, the following precautions should be taken:

I. Wash hands with soap and water before and after seeing the patient. Hand hygiene with soap and water is essential because alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not effective against C. difficile spores.

II. Use bleach to clean the equipment and room. Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) is effective in killing C. difficile spores and preventing transmission.

V. Use gloves and a gown when entering the room. Healthcare workers should wear gloves and a gown when entering the room of a patient with C. difficile infection to prevent contamination of their hands and clothing.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - I and III: Regular antiseptic is not effective in getting rid of spores, so handwashing with soap and water is essential.

Option C - I–V: Airborne precautions are not required.

Option D - II, III, and V: Chlorine-containing cleaning agents or sporicidal agents should be used to clean the room and equipment.

She has a history of Grave’s disease, epilepsy, depression, and generalized anxiety disorder for which she takes propylthiouracil (PTU), valproic acid, fluoxetine, and clonazepam, respectively. The pleural fluid was found to be exudative and contain 15% eosinophils. Which of the following drugs is most likely associated with this patient’s eosinophilic pleural effusion?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old female is being evaluated for the recent onset of pleuritic chest pain. She has a history of Grave’s disease, epilepsy, depression, and generalized anxiety disorder for which she takes propylthiouracil (PTU), valproic acid, fluoxetine, and clonazepam, respectively. The pleural fluid was found to be exudative and contain 15% eosinophils. Which of the following drugs is most likely associated with this patient’s eosinophilic pleural effusion?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Propylthiouracil (PTU): Pleural fluid eosinophilia by definition contains > 10 % eosinophils and may occur with a number of pulmonary conditions which may introduce air or blood into the pleural space, neoplasms, and infections. Drugs are also a plausible cause, as there are 25 drugs which are associated with development of eosinophilic pleural effusions, the most common drugs being PTU, sulfasalazine, and warfarin. The appearance from the time of initiating the drug and the effusion is typically two months. Treatment consists of discontinuing the offending agent and administering oral glucocorticoids. Incorrect Options: Option A - Fluoxetine: This selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used for depression is not typically associated with eosinophilic pleural effusions. Its most common side effects include nausea, upset stomach, diarrhea, dry mouth, sleep problems, and weight changes. While drug-induced lupus can be associated with pleural effusion, fluoxetine is not typically implicated in this condition. Option B - Valproic acid: This medication is primarily used to treat epilepsy and bipolar disorder. While it can have numerous side effects, such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or tremor, it is not typically associated with eosinophilic pleural effusions. Option D - Clonazepam: This benzodiazepine medication is primarily used for treating anxiety and panic disorders, as well as certain types of seizures. It can have side effects like drowsiness, dizziness, and loss of coordination, but it is not typically linked to eosinophilic pleural effusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after falling at home. In the emergency department, he has 2 more seizures and subsequently is treated with 2mg of IV lorazepam. A non-contrast CT brain is unremarkable. While waiting for a room on the neurology floor, the patient had a 3-minute generalized seizure that resolved after an additional 2mg of lorazepam. The patient was transferred to the ICU and had another seizure. He is loaded with phenytoin and is stable with no further seizures for the next 30 minutes. The patient’s vital signs are within normal limits, with the exception of a blood pressure of 140/90. He is obtunded, does not respond to verbal commands, has minimal withdrawal to painful stimuli, and shows minimal reflexes. On cranial nerve examination, he has tonic ocular deviation to the right. He has no history of seizures and was in good health before this hospitalization. What diagnostic test would be most useful at this time?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - EEG: As generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) progresses, the clinical seizures become increasingly disorganized and difficult to distinguish from interictal activity. In stage 3 of Treisman’s stages of the evolution of GCSE, clinical manifestations are described as frequent or continuous tonic or clonic activity, often confined to eyes, face, or hands. An EEG is critical to obtain immediately to determine if this patient is having continuous seizures since prolonged activity will result in neuronal cell death. Incorrect Options: Option A - MRI brain: While an MRI of the brain is an important diagnostic test, especially in the evaluation of new-onset seizures, it is not the most useful test at this time. The patient has already had a non-contrast CT of the brain, which was unremarkable, ruling out any acute hemorrhage or mass effect. An MRI may be considered later to evaluate for more subtle structural abnormalities or possible underlying causes of the seizures, but it is not the most urgent test at this moment. Option B - Spinal fluid analysis: Spinal fluid analysis may be indicated in certain cases of seizures, especially when there is a suspicion of encephalitis or other central nervous system infections. However, in this case, the patient's clinical presentation and history do not strongly suggest an infectious etiology. Additionally, spinal fluid analysis is not the most urgent test in the evaluation of status epilepticus. The priority at this time is to manage and control the ongoing seizures and assess for any immediate life-threatening complications. Option D - Arterial blood gas: Arterial blood gas (ABG) is a useful test in the evaluation of patients with seizures, especially if there is a concern for metabolic or respiratory acidosis. questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with recurring palpitations, chest pressure, and shortness of breath while walking. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol consumption and no significant medical history. Physical exam shows elevated jugular venous pulsations, lung crackles, S3 gallop, and pitting oedema below the knees. The patient's vital signs reveal a pulse of 110/min, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. What is the best next step in managing the underlying cause of the patient's current condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presents with recurring palpitations, chest pressure, and shortness of breath while walking. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol consumption and no significant medical history. Physical exam shows elevated jugular venous pulsations, lung crackles, S3 gallop, and pitting oedema below the knees. The patient's vital signs reveal a pulse of 110/min, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. What is the best next step in managing the underlying cause of the patient's current condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Alcohol Abstinence: This patient's history and symptoms point toward diagnosing dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to alcohol usage. The best choice to address the underlying cause of this patient’s clinical condition is to abstain from alcohol given that he has a 30-year history of alcohol consumption. Alcohol is directly toxic to the myocardium and decreases the contractile strength of the heart muscles. It also contributes to the dilation of the ventricles thus leading to dilated cardiomyopathy. If alcohol avoidance is done early, the damage is reversible and the myocardium can resume normal function. Jugular venous distention, lung crackles, S3 gallop and pitting oedema below the knees and tachycardia are common presentations seen in the case of dilated cardiomyopathy. A laterally displaced apical impulse and mitral regurgitation murmur can also be seen in such a case however, these are not reported in this case. Other etiologies of dilated cardiomyopathy include Chagas disease, cocaine use, beriberi, hemochromatosis, titin gene mutation, HIV, and Coxsackie B virus infection. Chronic atrial fibrillation and endocrinopathies like acromegaly, pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism are other conditions that result in this disorder. Incorrect Options: Option B- Salt and fluid restriction: These measures may temporarily help improve the symptoms for this patient as he shows signs of volume overload like oedema, jugular venous distention and crackles, but this will not treat the underlying cause of this patient’s condition. Only alcohol abstinence is going to treat the underlying cause. Option C- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor therapy: An Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is a first-line medication in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy to improve symptoms. However, this medication does nothing to improve the underlying cause or alter the pathophysiology behind this patient’s issue. Option D-Thiamine Substitution: Thiamine substitution would be beneficial for patients who are suffering from wet beriberi. This patient does not show any symptoms like peripheral neuropathy or confusion. This patient is at risk for B1 deficiency, but that is not the case, as his lack of symptoms shows. @Neet_pg_bot

On baseline investigations, serum sodium levels were 165mEq/L, blood glucose was 190mg/dl and serum ketones were negative. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema: In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema:

  • In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink
  • Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia
  • When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up
  • This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction
  • Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour
  • So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs and symptoms of cerebral edema like seizures or any neurologic dysfunction is important

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Monitoring blood glucose level:

  • Monitoring blood glucose levels is important in diabetic patients if they present with high blood glucose levels and positive serum ketones to manage the diabetic ketoacidosis
  • If the blood glucose level is mildly elevated and ketones are negative then blood glucose level monitoring is less important than the management of hypernatremia and its complications in these patients

Option B- Monitoring serum ketones level:

  • Serum ketones are monitored in patients when the presentation is of diabetic ketoacidosis like the fruity smell of the breath, acidic pH, positive serum ketones, and high blood glucose level level
  • If the blood glucose level is normal and ketones are negative then serum ketones monitoring is unnecessary

Option D- Monitoring for urine output:

  • Urine output monitoring is important in severe hypovolemia, decreased blood pressure, and oliguria
  • If the blood pressure and urine output are slightly decreased then monitoring is of secondary importance as compared to monitoring for signs of cerebral edema

questions.stem: Which of the following forms of thalassemia is typically not compatible with life?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following forms of thalassemia is typically not compatible with life?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha Thalassemia - Hemoglobin Barts: Hemoglobin Barts, also known as Hb Barts or γ4 tetramers, is a type of alpha thalassemia. It occurs when all four alpha-globin genes are deleted or severely mutated. This condition leads to the absence of functional alpha-globin chains, which are necessary for the production of normal adult hemoglobin (HbA). Fetuses affected by Hemoglobin Barts usually do not survive to term, and if they are born, they often die shortly after birth due to severe anemia and tissue hypoxia. The lack of functional alpha-globin chains results in the formation of gamma-globin tetramers (Hb Barts) that cannot adequately carry oxygen. This inability to transport oxygen contributes to the severe health issues associated with this condition. Incorrect Options: Option B - Alpha Thalassemia - Hemoglobin H Disease: Hemoglobin H disease results from the deletion of three alpha-globin genes, leaving only one functional alpha-globin gene. Individuals with Hemoglobin H disease can survive but often experience moderate to severe anemia and may require regular blood transfusions. Their life expectancy varies depending on the severity of the condition. Option C - Beta Thalassemia - Beta Thalassemia Major: Beta thalassemia major, also known as Cooley's anemia, is a severe form of beta thalassemia. It occurs when both beta-globin genes are mutated or absent, leading to the lack of functional beta-globin chains required to form HbA. Individuals with beta thalassemia major require lifelong blood transfusions and chelation therapy to manage iron overload resulting from frequent transfusions. With proper treatment, they can survive into adulthood, although the quality of life may be significantly impacted. Option D - Beta Thalassemia - Beta Thalassemia Intermedia: Beta thalassemia intermedia is a milder form of beta thalassemia. Individuals with beta thalassemia intermedia often require occasional or no blood transfusions, as they can produce some functional beta-globin chains. Life expectancy varies widely in this group, and individuals may experience moderate to severe symptoms but generally have a better prognosis compared to beta thalassemia major. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Length-time bias: Length-time bias is an error which occurs due to measuring a time interval which is to short, possible over-representing longer disease processes. This error is especially applicable to lung cancers, which have a wide variability of growth rates. Incorrect Options: Option A - Centripetal bias: Centripetal bias occurs when a study cohort is analyzed through a specific institution or center that may not be representative of the broader population. This can lead to biased results that may not be applicable to the general population. Option B - Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias occurs when a disease is detected earlier through screening or diagnostic tests, but this early detection does not necessarily lead to improved outcomes. This bias can make it appear that a screening test is effective in prolonging survival, when in fact, it may only be detecting the disease earlier without providing any actual benefit in terms of survival. Option D - Reporting bias: Reporting bias refers to the selective inclusion or exclusion of results in a study, which can lead to a distortion of the true relationship between variables. This bias can arise if researchers or journals choose to publish only positive or significant results, while neglecting to publish negative or non-significant findings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Serum iron 15 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, serum ferritin 10 μg/L, percent saturation 7%
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Serum iron 15 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, serum ferritin 10 μg/L, percent saturation 7%: This set of lab values is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia caused by chronic blood loss, such as from a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Serum Iron: Low serum iron levels are expected in iron deficiency anemia because the body's iron stores are depleted due to chronic bleeding. TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity): Elevated TIBC indicates that the body is trying to compensate for low iron levels by increasing its capacity to bind and transport iron. Serum Ferritin: Ferritin is an indicator of the body's iron stores. In this case, the low ferritin level reflects depleted iron stores. Percent Saturation: The percent saturation of transferrin (serum iron/TIBC x 100) is also low due to the insufficient amount of iron available to bind with transferrin. Incorrect Options: Option B - Serum Iron 100 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 10 μg/L, Percent Saturation 7%: While the low ferritin and percent saturation are consistent with iron deficiency, a serum iron level of 100 μg/dL is not indicative of iron deficiency anemia, especially considering the low ferritin level and low percent saturation. Iron levels are expected to be low in iron deficiency anemia. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Measurement of glomerular filtration rate (GFR): The diagnosis of CKD involves a combination of clinical assessment, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. The following are the steps involved in the diagnosis of CKD: Assessment of risk factors: The first step in the diagnosis of CKD is to assess the patient's risk factors, including age, family history, medical history, and lifestyle factors. Evaluation of symptoms: The next step is to evaluate the patient's symptoms, such as fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, and swelling in the legs and ankles. Measurement of kidney function: Kidney function is typically measured using a blood test that measures the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the level of creatinine in the blood. The GFR is a measure of how well the kidneys are filtering waste from the blood, while creatinine is a waste product that is normally excreted by the kidneys. Urine tests: Urine tests are also used to diagnose CKD. The presence of protein or blood in the urine can indicate kidney damage. Imaging studies: Imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI may be used to look for structural abnormalities in the kidneys. Biopsy: In some cases, a kidney biopsy may be necessary to diagnose CKD. A small sample of kidney tissue is removed and examined under a microscope to look for signs of damage or disease. Incorrect Options: Option A- Renal biopsy: Renal biopsy is not the initial step in the diagnosis of CKD, as renal biopsy is an invasive procedure and is usually reserved for cases in which the diagnosis is unclear or for patients with suspected glomerulonephritis. Option B- Imaging studies of the kidneys: Imaging studies of the kidneys may be useful in determining the cause of CKD, but it is not the initial step in the diagnosis. Option D- Measurement of urine electrolyte levels: Measurement of urine electrolyte levels is not the initial step in the diagnosis of CKD, as it does not provide information about the degree of kidney function. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - The gastric balloon is inflated first and suction is applied to both ports; if blood continues to return, the esophageal balloon should be inflated: A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube can be lifesaving and so emergency physicians should be familiar with its use. Option D - Any coagulopathies should be corrected before placing the device: As this procedure is generally undertaken as a life-saving measure when medical therapy has failed, one should not wait to correct any coagulopathies before placement. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Accumulation of organic acids Kidneys are the vital organs of the human body that play an important role in the filtration of blood and excretion of metabolic wastes. Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. Some of the symptoms of kidney failure are decreased urine output, fatigue, muscle cramps, fluid overload, nausea, vomiting, dry skin, etc. Incorrect options: Option A: Ketones accumulation Ketone accumulation can also result in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. Ketones are accumulated in the body in diabetes. It is a common condition in type I diabetes mellitus in which insulin is deficient. Option C: Accumulation of salicylates Aspirin is usually used for its analgesic and antiplatelet effect for the management of different diseases. The aspirin is also called salicylates. The salicylate overdose can result in metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. It can also cause respiratory alkalosis initially because of the increased respiratory drive. Option D: Accumulation of formate Methanol is an alcohol that is used in antifreeze, perfumes, carburetor cleaners, etc. Methanol toxicity occurs because of unintentional ingestion of methanol. The methanol is converted into formaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. The formaldehyde is further converted into formate by the aldehyde dehydrogenase. It can also cause increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. @Neet_pg_bot

A physical examination of the lungs demonstrates decreased breath sounds and wheezing bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination reveals a loud second heart sound. His abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. His liver is slightly enlarged. Examination of the extremities reveals 3+ lower-extremity edema. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.35, PO2 53 mmHg, PCO2 59 mmHg, and HCO3 31 mEq/L. The patient is admitted to the medical unit and receives methylprednisolone and azithromycin as part of his treatment regimen. Which of the following has shown the greatest evidence of direct mortality improvement in COPD?
questions.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old man with COPD is brought to the ER with shortness of breath. Upper lung predominant emphysema is not present. He admits to frequent hospitalizations (at least 5 in the past 3 months) for COPD exacerbations. He complains of progressively worsening of shortness of breath and a productive cough with copious amounts of yellow-green sputum. The patient is a lifelong smoker (90 pack-years). Comorbid medical conditions include hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He is currently on ipratropium, aspirin, nitroglycerin, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and omeprazole, in addition to home oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal cannula.
The patient's vitals are as follows: temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius (99.4 degrees Fahrenheit), blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, pulse 116/min, and respirations 29/min. A physical examination of the lungs demonstrates decreased breath sounds and wheezing bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination reveals a loud second heart sound. His abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. His liver is slightly enlarged. Examination of the extremities reveals 3+ lower-extremity edema. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.35, PO2 53 mmHg, PCO2 59 mmHg, and HCO3 31 mEq/L. The patient is admitted to the medical unit and receives methylprednisolone and azithromycin as part of his treatment regimen. Which of the following has shown the greatest evidence of direct mortality improvement in COPD?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oxygen therapy: Oxygen therapy is the only treatment modality that definitively decreases morbidity and mortality significantly in patients with COPD. Criteria for initiation of oxygen therapy include the following: resting PaO 2 <55 mmHg, oxygen saturation <88%, PaO 2 <59 mmHg with evidence of cor pulmonale, erythrocytosis, and hematocrit >55%. ATC is a rare and aggressive form of thyroid carcinoma associated with a poor prognosis. It is often characterised by rapid growth, invasion of surrounding tissues, and distant metastasis. Targeted therapies may also address specific molecular abnormalities in the tumour. Palliative care may be necessary in cases of advanced ATC that are not responsive to treatment , but it is not the primary management option. questions.stem: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk: Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible . Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death: The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause Is highly unconscious and unresponsive Requires ventilation No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation. Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed. These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions. The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death. An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death. Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex: The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death. These reflexes are: Pupillary Corneal Gag (pharyngeal) Tracheal (cough) Oculovestibular (caloric) Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration: The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner: Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration. During this time, the arterial PO 2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg ) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation. 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea. Option D - Absence of cough: A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Is highly unconscious and unresponsive
    • Requires ventilation
    • No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation.
    • Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies
  • With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed.
  • These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions.
  • The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death.
  • An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death.
  • Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex:

  • The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death.
  • These reflexes are:
    • Pupillary
    • Corneal
    • Gag (pharyngeal)
    • Tracheal (cough)
    • Oculovestibular (caloric)

Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration:

  • The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner:
    • Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration.
    • During this time, the arterial PO2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation.
    • 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea.

Option D - Absence of cough:

  • A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death.

questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Valsalva manoeuvre: Vagal manoeuvres are simple techniques used to terminate an episode of PSVT by stimulating the vagus nerve, which slows down the heart rate. These manoeuvres are safe and effective for most patients and can be performed in inpatient and outpatient settings. Some examples of vagal manoeuvres include: Valsalva manoeuvre: This involves forcefully exhaling against a closed airway ( e.g., by pinching the nose and closing the mouth) for 10-15 seconds. This increases intrathoracic pressure , stimulating the vagus nerve and slowing the heart rate. Carotid sinus massage: This involves applying gentle pressure to the carotid artery in the neck for 5-10 seconds. This can activate the baroreceptor reflex, which slows down the heart rate. Cold water immersion of the face involves splashing cold water on the face or immersing the face in cold water for a few seconds. This stimulates the trigeminal nerve, stimulating the vagus nerve and slows the heart rate. Gagging: This involves stimulating the gag reflex by touching the back of the throat with a tongue depressor or toothbrush. This can activate the vagus nerve and slow down the heart rate. Vagal manoeuvres are generally safe, but they should not be performed in patients with certain conditions, such as carotid artery disease, a history of stroke, or glaucoma. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pneumatic compression stockings: Pneumatic compression stockings, also known as compression stockings or compression socks, are commonly used to prevent deep vein thrombosis in hospitalized patients. They work by applying pressure to the legs to improve blood flow. While they can be beneficial for preventing blood clots, they are ineffective in terminating an episode of PSVT. Option C - Oxygen therapy: Oxygen therapy is commonly used in the emergency department to treat hypoxia or respiratory distress. While it can be helpful in certain situations, it is ineffective for terminating an episode of PSVT. Option D - Intravenous fluids: Intravenous fluids may be used in the emergency department to correct hypovolemia or electrolyte imbalances, which can contribute to developing PSVT. questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female presents to the emergency department with weakness, fatigue, and dizziness. She reports a history of hyperpigmentation and has a recent diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis. On examination, she appears dehydrated, and her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a low cortisol level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Addison's disease: The clinical picture of this patient is suggestive of Addison's disease which is the most common cause of Chronic Primary Adrenal Insufficiency in developed nations. Addison's disease is a condition where the adrenal glands do not produce enough cortisol and sometimes aldosterone. The clinical features of Addison's disease include: Fatigue and weakness: One of the most common symptoms of Addison's disease is fatigue, weakness, and malaise. Patients may feel tired even after getting enough rest. Weight loss and decreased appetite: Patients with Addison's disease may experience weight loss and decreased appetite. Hyperpigmentation: This is the darkening of the skin, most commonly seen on the face, neck, and hands. It is caused by an increase in melanin production because melano cortical stimulating hormone (MSH) is produced along with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from pro-opiomelanocortin. Hypotension: Low blood pressure due to sodium loss and iso-osmotic water loss is a common feature of Addison's disease. Patients may feel dizzy or faint when they stand up. Salt cravings: Patients may experience salt cravings due to the low aldosterone levels which results in sodium loss. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea: These symptoms may occur due to the body's inability to regulate electrolyte balance and water. Muscle and joint pain: Patients with Addison's disease may experience muscle and joint pain due to the lack of cortisol in the body. Depression and irritability: Low cortisol levels can also cause emotional changes, such as depression and irritability. Incorrect Options: Option A - Graves’ disease: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder causing the thyroid gland to produce excessive thyroid hormone. Symptoms include weight loss, increased appetite, palpitations, rapid heartbeat, tremors, sweating, heat intolerance, goitre, eye problems, skin changes, emotional changes, menstrual irregularities, weakness, and muscle wasting.The clinical features of hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and low cortisol levels in addition to weakness, fatigue, dizziness and hyperpigmentation are suggestive of Addison disease. Option B - Hashimoto thyroiditis: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the thyroid gland, leading to hypothyroidism. The condition results from the "antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies." and damaging the thyroid gland, which results in the gland's inability to produce enough thyroid hormones. This leads to symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain, constipation, depression, and dry skin. However, Addison's disease is an autoimmune disease that primarily affects the adrenal glands, leading to a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone. Both conditions share some clinical features, such as fatigue and muscle weakness, but the main different clinical features are: Hyperpigmentation of the skin, especially in sun-exposed areas Salt cravings Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) Nausea and vomiting Dizziness or lightheadedness upon standing up (orthostatic hypotension) Option D - Cushing disease: Cushing's disease is a condition caused by the overproduction of cortisol hormone by the pituitary gland. The excess cortisol can cause a wide range of symptoms, including weight gain, high blood pressure, muscle weakness, and increased risk of infections. While Cushing’s disease and Addison’s disease share some similar features like fatigue, weakness, changes in weight, mood swings and increased risk of infection, there are some key differences for example, Cushing disease can cause symptoms such as high blood pressure, a round "moon" face, and a buffalo hump on the back, while Addison's disease can cause symptoms such as low blood pressure, hyperpigmentation of the skin, and salt cravings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Brain MRI: The next best investigation to guide acute management in this case is a brain MRI. The patient's presentation of left-sided weakness affecting the face, arm, and leg, double vision, and profound ataxia suggests a possible posterior circulation stroke, involving the vertebrobasilar artery territory. CT imaging is less sensitive in detecting early ischemic changes in the posterior fossa compared to brain MRI, especially when performed within a short time window from symptom onset. Brain MRI, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequence, is highly sensitive and specific in detecting acute ischemic changes and can provide more detailed information about the location and extent of the stroke. It can also help rule out other potential etiologies, such as posterior fossa tumors or demyelinating disorders. Therefore, a brain MRI is the most appropriate next investigation to guide acute management in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carotid Duplex Ultrasonography: Carotid duplex ultrasonography is a non-invasive imaging technique used to assess the blood flow in the carotid arteries. While it is valuable in evaluating the carotid arteries for stenosis or occlusion in patients with suspected ischemic stroke, it may not be the most appropriate initial investigation in this case. The patient's symptoms of left-sided weakness, double vision, and ataxia suggest a posterior circulation stroke and carotid duplex ultrasonography primarily focuses on the anterior circulation. Therefore, it may not provide sufficient information to guide acute management in this specific case. Option C - Cerebral Catheter Angiography: Cerebral catheter angiography, also known as digital subtraction angiography (DSA), is an invasive procedure that involves injecting a contrast dye directly into the cerebral arteries to evaluate the blood vessels' structure and detect any abnormalities, such as an aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. While DSA can provide detailed information about the cerebral vasculature, it is an invasive procedure and is not typically the initial investigation in acute stroke management. Moreover, the CT angiography already performed showed no large vessel occlusion, which reduces the urgency for catheter angiography. Option D - CT Perfusion Scan: CT perfusion scan is an imaging technique used to evaluate cerebral blood flow and assess brain tissue viability. It provides valuable information about the extent of ischemic tissue and can help identify areas of salvageable tissue (penumbra). However, in this case, the patient's symptoms and NIHSS score suggest a large vessel occlusion, and the CT angiography has already ruled out such an occlusion. Therefore, CT perfusion may not add significant benefit to guide acute management in this specific scenario. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Start the patient on 4 drug intensive phase treatment
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start the patient on 4 drug intensive phase therapy: This patient has clinical features consistent with Active pulmonary tuberculosis, including a persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, a left upper lobe infiltrate on chest x-ray, and AFB seen on sputum microscopy. A positive Mantoux tuberculin skin test further supports the diagnosis. The most appropriate next step in management is to start the patient on 4 drug therapy for 2 months (intensive phase). Recommended first line treatment includes isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. This is followed by continuation phase treatment with isoniazid and rifampin for 4-6 months. Incorrect Options: Option A - Start the patient on isoniazid therapy alone: Isoniazid monotherapy is not recommended due to the risk of developing resistant strains of mycobacterium tuberculosis. Option C - Refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation: It may be appropriate in certain cases, especially in complicated cases, but in this case, the patient can be managed by a primary care provider. Option D - Start the patient on pyrazinamide and ethambutol therapy: Pyrazinamide and ethambutol are typically used in combination with isoniazid and rifampin during intensive phase therapy but not in isolation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Load with 20 mg/kg of IV fosphenytoin: The patient’s liver dysfunction may slow her metabolism of phenytoin, and drug levels will need to be followed closely after initial dosing, however fosphenytoin does not cause liver toxicity and is a great second line loading medication for status epilepticus. In general, this “second line” medication should be given in parallel with the second dose of benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam). Incorrect Options: Option A - Load with 40 mg/kg of IV sodium valproate: Valproate is contraindicated in this patient given her hepatic dysfunction. questions.stem: Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion resulting in transfusion refractoriness?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion resulting in transfusion refractoriness?

options.label: A
options.text: 52 year old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor

options.label: B
options.text: 52 year old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor

options.label: C
options.text: 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor

options.label: D

questions.answerText: 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor
questions.solution: Correct Option C - 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor: Generally, multiparous women are more likely than men or nulliparous women to develop alloimmunization to platelets. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor puts her at an even higher risk, as she may have developed antibodies to the child's father's HLA antigens during her pregnancy. Most cases (~2/3) of platelet refactoriness are NOT due to alloimmunization. However, in cases that are, most are due to antibodies that are created in response to HLA class I antigens on leukocytes or platelets. These antibodies can exist in multiparous women due to maternal-fetal HLA incompatibility during pregnancy. Fetal HLA class I antigens inherited from the father are recognized by the mother as foreign. Multiple pregnancies will put the patient at a higher risk of developing such antibodies. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor greatly increases the risk of re-presenting HLA class I antigens to antibodies which she has developed.Platelet alloimmunization can also occur in patients who have received multiple transfusions or due to antibodies to platelet specific antigens (human platelet antigens). Incorrect Options: Option A - 52-year-old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor: Alloimmunization to platelet transfusion is more common in multiparous women, as they are exposed to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. In this case, the patient has not been pregnant before (G0P0), which lowers her likelihood of developing alloantibodies. Additionally, her husband's HLA antigens are less likely to trigger an immune response compared to antigens from her own offspring. Option B - 52 -year-old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor: This patient is also a nulliparous woman (G0P0), reducing her risk of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion. The likelihood of developing alloantibodies is higher in multiparous women due to exposure to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. Option D - 52-year-old G4P4 female with a random platelet donor: While this patient is multiparous (G4P4) and has a higher likelihood of developing alloantibodies, the key difference compared to option C is the donor. In this case, the donor is random, meaning the donor's HLA antigens are not specifically associated with those of her offspring. The risk of developing antibodies against random donor HLA antigens is lower compared to antibodies against her son's HLA antigens. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Urinary retention Up to 20% of ipratropium can be absorbed given as MDI can be absorbed via mucosal membranes of the mouth or systemic absorption through the pulmonary circulation. Consequently, some systemic side effect can be possible. Anticholinergic agents are known to cause urinary retention. In pooled analyzed of 19 randomized trial symptoms of urinary retention was more frequently present in a patient taking inhaled anticholinergic that control group. On the other hand UPLIFT trial showed no-statistically significant increase in the rate of urinary retention. Finally, in small trial 25 patient with BPH, no exacerbation of symptoms was noted. Consequently, the patient should be counseled that urinary retention might occur, but it is not universal complication. Incorrect Options: Options B - Immunosuppression: This is not a typical side effect of anticholinergic medications such as ipratropium. Immunosuppression is more commonly seen with long-term use of corticosteroids, which can suppress the body's immune response. Options C - Dry mouth: While it is true that anticholinergic medications can cause dry mouth, this is typically a local side effect due to the medication acting on the muscarinic receptors in the salivary glands to reduce saliva production. However, in the case of inhaled ipratropium, the medication is mainly acting on the receptors in the lungs and not the salivary glands. Therefore, while dry mouth can occur, it is less common and generally not considered a systemic side effect. Option D - Hair loss: Hair loss is not a known side effect of anticholinergic medications like ipratropium. Hair loss can occur due to various reasons, including genetics, certain diseases, stress, and the use of certain medications, but ipratropium is not known to cause this. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Low serum ceruloplasmin levels: The patient's depression, psychosis (hearing voices), tremor and gait disturbance combined with the characteristic eye finding of Keyser-Fleisher rings, suggests Wilson disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene. ATP7B is a copper-transporting protein that is primarily expressed in the liver, where it facilitates the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, a copper-containing protein that is secreted into the blood. Defective ATP7B gene results in defective copper transport and metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in liver leading to cirrhosis. Copper is subsequently deposited in other organs, primarily the basal ganglia in the brain causing neurological dysfunction such as tremors, gait dysfunction, depression and psychosis. Inability of defective ATP7B protein to incorporate copper into apoceruloplasmin leads to low serum ceruloplasmin concentration. Low serum ceruloplasmin is diagnostic for Wilson disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - High serum ferritin: Elevated serum ferritin levels are a common finding in hemochromatosis that can lead to hepatosplenomegaly and signs of liver failure, as well as neurological symptoms if hepatic encephalopathy develops. However, the presence of ascites or peripheral edema would be expected in cases of chronic liver disease. Additionally, hemochromatosis typically presents in patients over 30 years of age and may involve other features, such as skin pigmentation, joint pain, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy and testicular atrophy in males. Option C - Elevated number of CAG repeats: Having an elevated number of CAG repeats on genetic testing is diagnostic of Huntington's disease (HD), which can result in impaired motor abilities such as gait disturbance and tremors. Typical clinical features of HD, including chorea, athetosis, sensory deficits, and autonomic symptoms like sweating and urinary problems, are not present in this patient. Moreover, HD does not affect the liver. Option D - Enlarged ventricles on CT scan of the brain: Enlarged ventricles on brain imaging is indicative of hydrocephalus. Normal pressure hydrocephalus mostly occurs in older individuals and is often associated with difficulty walking. However, since this patient does not exhibit other typical symptoms of NPH like dementia or urinary incontinence, it is less likely to be the underlying cause. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old lady presented in the ER complaining of sudden onset palpitation, sweating and dizziness. She also had a previous history of these kinds of episodes. O/E, her extremities are cold, and her blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the best next step in managing this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- I/V adenosine: Patients presenting with palpitation, dizziness, hypotension and ECG showing absent P-wave with narrow QRS complex are most likely having supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). The best step in managing SVT is to terminate it using I/V adenosine. The patient's clinical presentation and underlying cause determine the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Some general SVT management strategies include: Vagal manoeuvres: These are simple manoeuvres that stimulate the vagus nerve and, in some cases, can help terminate SVT. Examples are the Valsalva manoeuvre, carotid sinus massage, and face immersion in cold water. Medications: Various medications can be used to control the heart rate or rhythm in SVT patients. The drug of choice is adenosine. Adenosine is a medication that slows the heart's electrical activity to stop supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Adenosine causes a transient block of the AV node, interrupting the reentry circuit responsible for SVT by binding to adenosine receptors in the heart. Electrical cardioversion delivers a synchronized shock to the heart to restore normal rhythm. It is usually reserved for patients who have refractory SVT. Catheter ablation: This is a minimally invasive procedure in which a catheter is inserted through a blood vessel into the heart, and radiofrequency energy is used to ablate the area of the heart responsible for the SVT. Many patients with recurrent or symptomatic SVT can benefit from it. Incorrect Options: Option A- I/V normal saline I/V normal saline is not the best step in managing this patient. I/V fluids can help to restore normal blood pressure in case of hypovolemic shock. This patient's low bp is due to SVT, not loss of plasma volume. So, the best next step for this patient is to terminate the SVT by using adenosine. Option B- I/V amiodarone I/V amiodarone can be used as a second-line agent to terminate the SVT. But due to its side effects, it is used only if the first-line agents are unavailable or ineffective. Option D- I/V labetalol: I/V labetalol is the drug of choice in case of a hypertension emergency. It is not useful to terminate SVT. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Drug induced lupus: Sulfasalazine is a combination of 5-aminosalicylic acid and sulfapyridine (a sulfonamide drug). Sulfonamides are a recognised cause of drug-induced lupus. Other common culprit drugs associated with a lupus-like syndrome include minocycline, TNF antagonists, procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, chlorpromazine, quinidine, methyldopa, phenytoin. The incidence of drug-induced lupus is equal between males and females and may be associated with slow acetylation status and HLA-DR41. Anti histone antibodies are positive in drug-induced lupus, but the test is not widely available, and often is unnecessary provided there is a suggestive history and positive ANA. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are not usually positive. Renal involvement in drug-induced lupus is rare, but may be seen with hydralazine. It is important to recognise drug-induced lupus as a separate entity from systemic lupus erythematosus and subacute cutaneous lupus, since the condition resolves on cessation of the offending drug, usually within days or a few weeks. ANA however may remain positive for months or years after exposure. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fixed Drug Eruption: Fixed drug eruption is characterized by recurrent skin lesions in the same location each time a specific drug is taken. These lesions appear as well-defined, round or oval patches or plaques that can be red or darkly pigmented. The lesions tend to recur at the same site with subsequent exposure to the drug. This diagnosis doesn't fit the patient's symptoms of arthralgia, photosensitive facial rash, pleuritic chest pain, and other systemic manifestations. Option C - Pyoderma Gangrenosum: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare skin disorder characterized by the development of painful, ulcerative skin lesions. These lesions typically start as pustules and rapidly progress to deep, necrotic ulcers with purplish or undermined edges. Pyoderma gangrenosum can occur in various conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatological disorders. The patient's rash doesn't match the description of pyoderma gangrenosum. Option D - Subacute Cutaneous Lupus: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) is a form of lupus that primarily affects the skin. It typically presents with annular or psoriasiform skin lesions, often in sun-exposed areas. While photosensitivity is a common feature of SCLE, the patient's symptoms and clinical presentation, including pleuritic chest pain, suggest a more systemic involvement. SCLE lesions are usually non-scarring and may resolve without scarring, which contrasts with the patient's oral ulcers. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 39-year-old lady with a 28-year history of type 1 diabetes with chronic poor glycaemic control has a most recent HbA1c of 86.9 mmol/mol (10.1%). Her current insulin regimen includes twice-daily Novomix 30 at doses of 34 units in the morning and 38 units in the evening. On examination, her blood pressure is 144/68 mmHg, her BMI is 23 kg/m2 and examination of her feet reveals reduced vibration, proprioception and thermosensation in both feet. Retinal screening reveals evidence of neovascularization in the left eye. Which of the following factors has been shown to have an important role in regulating retinal capillary blood flow?

Her current insulin regimen includes twice-daily Novomix 30 at doses of 34 units in the morning and 38 units in the evening. On examination, her blood pressure is 144/68 mmHg, her BMI is 23 kg/m2 and examination of her feet reveals reduced vibration, proprioception and thermosensation in both feet. Retinal screening reveals evidence of neovascularization in the left eye. Which of the following factors has been shown to have an important role in regulating retinal capillary blood flow?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Contractile action of pericytes: The retinal pericytes regulate retinal capillary blood flow but they are often damaged and reduced in number in patients with diabetic retinopathy leading to disordered blood flow regulation and increased shear stress on the vessel walls which drives the pathogenesis of retinopathy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Contractile action of endothelial cells: While endothelial cells form the inner lining of blood vessels and play a role in regulating vascular tone, their contractile action is more relevant to larger blood vessels rather than capillaries. Option C - Local release of interleukins: Interleukins are a group of cytokines that play a role in the body's immune response and inflammation. While inflammation is involved in the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, interleukins do not directly regulate retinal capillary blood flow. Option D - Local release of nitric oxide: Nitric oxide is a vasodilator and can influence blood flow in blood vessels. However, its role in the regulation of retinal capillary blood flow is not as crucial as the contractile action of pericytes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male patient is newly diagnosed with minimally symptomatic COPD. He is at low risk of an exacerbation. Pulmonary function test shows no difference in FEV1 before and after inhaled short-term bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male patient is newly diagnosed with minimally symptomatic COPD. He is at low risk of an exacerbation. Pulmonary function test shows no difference in FEV1 before and after inhaled short-term bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Introduce steroids to sensitize airway to sympathomimetics

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the test after three months

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed

questions.answerText: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed: Short-acting bronchodilators provide the best relief of symptoms in COPD and should be prescribed for all patients with minimal symptoms and low risk of exacerbation. Bronchodilators induce long-term improvements in symptoms, exercise capacity, and airflow limitation, even in patients who do not have spirometric improvement after a test dose. Incorrect Options: Option A - Introduce steroids to sensitize airway to sympathomimetics: This option is not appropriate as it suggests the use of steroids to sensitize the airways to sympathomimetics. Steroids are not used for this purpose in COPD management. Steroids have anti-inflammatory effects and are typically reserved for patients with severe COPD or those experiencing exacerbations. In this patient with minimally symptomatic COPD and no evidence of bronchodilator responsiveness on pulmonary function testing, starting steroids is not indicated. Option B - Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness: This option is also not appropriate as it suggests avoiding sympathomimetics based on the lack of airway responsiveness on pulmonary function testing. Short-acting bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are the mainstay of treatment for relieving symptoms in COPD, regardless of the degree of airway responsiveness on testing. Many patients with COPD experience symptom relief and improved exercise capacity with short-acting bronchodilators, even if their FEV1 does not show significant improvement. Option C - Repeat the test after three months: Repeating the pulmonary function test after only three months is not necessary or indicated in this case. Pulmonary function testing is typically performed annually to monitor disease progression and response to treatment. In this patient with newly diagnosed minimally symptomatic COPD and low risk of exacerbation, the focus should be on symptom relief and appropriate management rather than frequent testing. @Neet_pg_bot
